## Toward a grammar of ideological disagreement beyond left and right

after.text: The task is not to abolish left and right. They are among the most durable and efficient heuristics in modern politics. Voters use them to infer large bundles of positions from a few cues, even though the cues and their meaning differ across people and countries.\[1\] The task is to build a vocabulary capable of decompressing them.

## I. From Essences to Arrangements

after.text: Michael Freeden’s morphological theory begins from this fact. Ideologies draw from a common field of contested political concepts (liberty, equality, authority, community, democracy, order) and give them determinate meaning by placing them into characteristic configurations.\[2\] Liberty means something different when equality is made its condition than when property is made its condition. Community means something different when organized around citizenship than when organized around ancestry. Democracy means something different when understood as plural contestation than when understood as the undivided will of a people.

Social democrats across countries share enough history and conceptual structure to constitute a recognizable family, but no checklist supplies necessary and sufficient conditions for every member. The first version of this framework made the classic taxonomist’s mistake: it optimized for exhaustive classification at the expense of language. Five binary dimensions yield thirty-two logical vertices. It is possible to give each one a precise name. It is also possible to make the result unusable. A phrase such as _universalist-institutional emancipatory egalitarianism_ identifies a point with admirable fidelity and no political life whatsoever.

after.text: The communal pole begins from special duties among members of bounded communities. It emphasizes reciprocity, shared history, social trust, sovereignty, and the proposition that solidarity requires a _we_ capable of sustaining it.

The academic literature often calls this the cosmopolitan–communitarian divide, especially in work on globalization, integration, borders, and sovereignty.\[4\] But communitarianism is not a synonym for ethnic nationalism. A bounded political community may be civic, constitutional, linguistic, religious, cultural, local, or ethnonational. These require secondary tags.

after.text: Multi-axis correctives to the spectrum are nearly as old as the complaint against it. The lineage runs from the Nolan chart through the Political Compass to the open-source 8values test and its axis-multiplying successors. The convergence with 8values in particular should be stated plainly: it measures four axes (Equality against Markets, Liberty against Authority, Tradition against Progress, Nation against Globe), and three of them carry, verbatim, the pole names used here.\[6\] The convergence is better read as evidence than as embarrassment. Independent attempts to decompress the spectrum keep finding the same questions, because these are the questions politics keeps returning to.

But the overlap must be named, because the difference lies in what is done with the answers. A test scores people: it asks its taker a battery of questions and returns a self. That is the wrong form for a political vocabulary. The objects that need describing are claims, laws, manifestos, parties, and governments—things that argue and act in public—not the private souls of quiz-takers. And a test has no discipline for its names. 8values contains, in embryo, this essay’s central move: after computing your coordinates it names your “closest match” ideology (coordinates first, family second) and then disowns the naming layer as “much less accurate than the values and axes,” advising users not to take it too seriously.\[6\] The disclaimer is the tell. The naming layer is not noise to be apologized for; it is where political language actually lives. What the test tradition lacks is not axes. It is a semantics for the names, which is what the rest of this essay builds.

The deeper challenge comes from the positions flanking any such framework. On one side stands the pragmatic defense of the single line: Bryan Caplan’s argument that the spectrum earns its keep because it tracks the political identities and conflicts that actually exist. On the other stand the eliminativists: Hyrum and Verlan Lewis, whose _The Myth of Left and Right_ is the strongest published version of this essay’s own opening move (left and right are tribal bundles, not philosophies), and also its standing refutation.\[7\] If bundling is the sin, the Lewises ask, why re-bundle at any scale? “There is more than one issue in politics.” Keep issues unbundled, as biology keeps species: “Why not just say ‘anti-market’ instead of ‘left-wing’?”

after.text: ## **IV. Separable but Bound**

If the five questions are analytically separable, they are certainly not empirically independent. Political attitudes do not arrive in independent boxes. They form coalitions, inherit institutions, respond to events, and become socially sorted. The literature is clear on at least two points: one dimension is often insufficient, since economic and cultural attitudes can be separated both conceptually and empirically; and no universal factor structure settles politics once and for all.\[8\]

after.text: The empirical bundles remain important, and here precision matters, because the data below were built by the tradition this essay is trying to decompress. The 2024 Chapel Hill Expert Survey, completed by 609 political scientists assessing 279 European parties, is organized around a two-dimensional model: economic left–right, plus the dimension Hooghe, Marks, and Wilson named GAL/TAN (green/alternative/libertarian against traditionalism/authority/nationalism).\[9\]\[10\] TAN welds together three of this essay’s questions by design: culture, coercion, and belonging. And Herbert Kitschelt supplied the standard explanation for why the weld holds: postindustrial party competition runs along a left-libertarian/right-authoritarian diagonal in that two-dimensional space.\[11\]

I constructed exploratory composites from the 2024 survey corresponding to the five questions; the variables are listed with the references so that the exercise can be checked.\[9\] Among European parties, culture, coercion, and belonging correlate pairwise at .84 to .90. Economy is related but more independent, at .47 to .56. The anti-establishment measures cut across everything else, including a slight negative correlation with market economics.

after.text: ## **V. What Populism Contains**

Cas Mudde’s influential definition treats populism as a “thin-centred” ideology that divides society between a pure people and a corrupt elite and demands that politics express the people’s general will.\[12\] This contains at least three claims:
1.  **Anti-establishment:** incumbent elites are corrupt or illegitimate.
2.  **Moral dualism:** the people and the elite form opposed moral camps.
3.  **Directism** (a term coined here for the purpose): legitimate rule should express an identifiable popular will.

The public axis remains **Insurgent ↔ Institutional**, with **Populist ↔ Establishment** as its familiar, deliberately approximate gloss. Underneath it, a rigorous profile records four facets: anti-establishment orientation (how captured or illegitimate are incumbent elites?); directism (should citizens decide directly or through representatives?); pluralism (are opposition and competing interests permanently legitimate?); and legitimation (is authority justified by popular will, expertise, law, tradition, or some combination?). None of these facets is an invention (political science already measures populist, pluralist, and elitist attitudes as separate scales\[15\]), but assembling them under a public gloss, rather than a score, is the point of the architecture.

after.text: ## **VI. Coordinates Before Categories**

before.text: ## VI. Coordinates Before Categories

after.text: One rule of interpretation before anything else: coordinates describe commitments and conduct, not souls. The natural first question (_what’s my number?_) is the quiz tradition’s question, and it is the wrong one. The objects worth scoring are arguments, programs, parties, and governments; a person is scored, if at all, only as the author of positions taken in public.

The address is not complete without four pieces of metadata: **salience** (how central is each question to the actor?), **confidence** (how strong and consistent is the evidence?), **time** (what campaign, governing period, or historical moment is being scored?), and **object** (a person, party, government, electorate, manifesto, or argument?). These distinctions prevent category errors. A party may be moderate on immigration because its position is genuinely balanced, because its factions cancel one another, because it speaks ambiguously, or because the issue is irrelevant to its project. Those are politically different facts, and the Chapel Hill survey accordingly records position, salience, internal dissent, and deliberate blurring separately.\[9\]

after.text: A prototype is not a checklist. It is a recognizable center of gravity. An actor can sit near two prototypes, occupy the edge of one, or combine a family with a modifier. This is how ordinary ideological language already works, and political science has a name for the semantics: radial categories, organized around a central case, with members related by resemblance rather than by necessary and sufficient conditions.\[16\]

after.text: The **welfare nationalist** demonstrates why left and right fail. Economic protection and social provision, bounded primarily by national membership: egalitarian within the community, exclusionary at its boundary, frequently paternalist in government, traditional in culture, and insurgent in rhetoric. Political science has studied the phenomenon for three decades under the name welfare chauvinism;\[17\] the family name used here is chosen to say what the position is for rather than only what it is against. Viktor Orbán’s Hungary sat near this neighborhood for sixteen years, with the caveat that its provision was workfare-flavored and flat-taxed: “welfare” in this family means provision bounded by membership, not redistributive generosity.

## **VIII. A Grammar, Not a Catalogue**

The lexicon becomes expressive through a small set of modifiers (populist, technocratic, progressive, traditionalist, welfare, market, civic, ethnonational, heterodox), used at most one at a time in ordinary prose: _populist libertarian_, _technocratic liberal_, _civic natcon_, _welfare nationalist_. When a third word seems necessary, stop naming and show the coordinates. This rule is more important than it appears. Labels gain explanatory power by excluding detail. Once a label attempts to encode all five dimensions, it becomes a coordinate string written in Latin.

## **IX. The Persistence of Left and Right**

## IX. The Persistence of Left and Right

after.text: Left and right persist because they solve a real coordination problem. Citizens cannot independently reconstruct every party’s position on every dispute. Coalitions need names. Media need contrasts. Political identities need inherited narratives. A one-word cue compresses policies, values, social groups, historical loyalties, and expectations about alliance. Recent research describes left–right inference in exactly these terms: people use a small number of predictive cues to place parties, though more politically sophisticated voters draw from a broader set of policies, values, and constituencies.\[1\] The spectrum is therefore not merely a philosophical error imposed on politics. It is an adaptation to limited attention.

There is also a deeper defense than coordination, and it deserves a named opponent rather than silence. Norberto Bobbio argued that left and right endure because they track a real and permanent divide: attitudes toward equality (a horizontal, egalitarian conception of society against a vertical, inegalitarian one).\[20\] If Bobbio is right, the five questions are one question wearing five masks, and this essay has multiplied entities without necessity. The framework’s answer is its cases. Equality-monism cannot score the welfare nationalist without remainder: egalitarian toward members, inegalitarian at the boundary is not a point on an equality line but an answer to two different questions—how much equality, and among whom. It cannot place Milei, whose radical anti-egalitarianism in economics arrives fused with an insurgent, anti-elite politics that speaks in the register Bobbio assigns to the left. The difficulty is not that Bobbio’s divide is unreal. It is that “equality” decomposes on contact: equality of what (economy), enforced how (coercion), against which inheritances (culture), among whom (belonging), decided by whom (system). Bobbio’s one question was five questions all along.

after.text: And this settles who the vocabulary is for. Not, primarily, voters: mass publics show little stable ideological structure of any dimensionality (the same survey research this essay leans on finds citizens’ attitudes far less constrained than elites’\[8\]), and a five-number address with metadata is no folk instrument. Pretending otherwise would repeat the quiz tradition’s mistake in a more demanding key, and it is part of why two decades of multi-axis tests have decorated the internet without displacing the spectrum: they addressed the wrong user. The vocabulary is for the people who produce political language (writers, analysts, editors, the arguing class), whose distinctions reach everyone else through the same cue-giving mechanism by which party positions reach voters in the first place.\[1\] The spectrum keeps the coordination job. The grammar works upstream, where the cues are written.
## **X. The Historicity of Families**

Pew Research Center’s 2026 American political typology illustrates both the promise and the limit of cluster-based naming. Using responses to thirty questions, Pew identified nine groups with memorable names such as _Leftward Progressives_, _Loyal Liberals_, _Order and Opportunity Left_, _Unconventional Right_, and _Faith First Conservatives_.\[21\] These groups are valuable because they describe actual clusters in a particular electorate at a particular time. They are not universal ideological species. A typology rerun in another country (or after a war, recession, migration crisis, religious revival, or technological transformation) would find different coalitions and require different names.
